result.summary: Hesiod advises the farmer to begin ploughing when the crane cries, to pray to Zeus and Demeter, and to plough and sow in good season. He then warns against idling in the smithy and describes the bitter month of Lenaeon, when Boreas blows, and how to dress and work to survive winter.

scenes.title: Ploughing season and sowing
scenes.summary: The crane's cry signals ploughing time. Hesiod tells the farmer to prepare his waggon timbers, plough early with his slaves, and pray to Zeus and Demeter for a heavy crop.
scenes.stakes: A farmer who is unprepared or late risks a poor harvest and having to beg from others.

scenes.title: Late ploughing and winter idleness
scenes.summary: Ploughing at the solstice brings a thin crop, though rain after the cuckoo's call can remedy lateness. Hesiod also warns against loafing in the smithy and tells the farmer to build barns in summer.
scenes.stakes: The idle or late farmer faces poverty and hardship in winter.

scenes.title: Boreas and the month Lenaeon
scenes.summary: Hesiod describes the north wind Boreas sweeping from Thrace, freezing beasts and old men while sparing the sheltered maiden. Animals flee for cover.
scenes.stakes: Beasts and men are in danger from the bitter cold.

scenes.title: Dressing and working for winter
scenes.summary: Hesiod gives advice on warm clothing, boots, cap and cloak, on finishing work before the mist and clouds come, and on feeding oxen and workers until spring returns.
scenes.stakes: Without proper clothing and care, the farmer's body and livestock suffer in the hardest month.

alias_notes.explanation: A title for Zeus as ruler of the gods on Olympus.
A riddling name for the octopus, which gnaws its foot in winter.
A riddle for an old man bent over a staff.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable maxim that good management is best and bad management worst.

analysis.text: The passage stresses timely work, foresight and diligence, and the dependence of farmers on Zeus's unpredictable will.
It preserves the practical farming calendar of early Greek smallholders, tied to the crane, the cuckoo and the month names such as Lenaeon.

legacy.text: Hesiod's farming calendar began the tradition of didactic poetry on agriculture, later developed by Virgil in the Georgics.

fun_facts.text: The riddling phrases 'Boneless One' and 'Three-legged One' are kennings for the octopus and the old man with a stick.

language_notes.text: The bracketed number 1317 is a footnote marker from the edition, not part of Hesiod's text. 'She give' is a typo for 'she gives'.
'Fallow broken up in the summer' means land left unplanted and ploughed in summer; it 'will not belie your hopes' by failing to yield.
'Soother of children' is obscure; probably it means a full harvest from fallow land keeps children fed and content.
'Zeus of the Earth' is Zeus in his underground, chthonic aspect, invoked for crops alongside Demeter, goddess of grain.
'Ween' is archaic for 'suppose' or 'think'; 'garnered substance' means the stored grain.
'The Olympian himself' refers to Zeus, who dwells on Olympus and ultimately decides whether the harvest succeeds.
"Solstice" here is the winter solstice (Greek trope), when the sun turns; ploughing then is far too late. The number 1319 is a footnote marker.
The cuckoo's first call signals spring; the "third day" rain, an ox-hoof deep, means soil moistened enough for late ploughing to catch up.
The smithy was a warm public gathering place where idle men chatted in winter; Hesiod treats it as a temptation to waste time.
"Chafe a swollen foot with a shrunk hand" depicts a starving, idle man rubbing his swollen, chilblained foot with a wasted hand.
Lenaeon is the coldest month of the Greek farming year, roughly January–February. "Fit to skin an ox" means so cruel they flay cattle.
The "Boneless One" is the octopus, which was thought to gnaw its own foot in winter when it lacks food.
"Dusky men" probably means Ethiopians or southern peoples, to whom the sun goes in winter, leaving Greece with weaker light.
The "Three-legged One" is an old man walking with a staff, echoing the riddle of the Sphinx.
"Thick woof on thin warp" means weaving heavy cross-threads through fine lengthwise threads to make a dense, warm felt-like cloth.

context_notes.text: The crane's autumn migration south was a traditional farming calendar sign, marking the time to plough and sow.
Greek farm waggons were built from many separate wooden parts, so timber had to be gathered and seasoned in advance.
A mattock is a heavy hoe-like tool; here the slave covers the sown seed with earth so birds cannot eat it.
Zeus holds the aegis, a divine shield or goatskin cloak symbolizing his power over storms and weather.
Boreas is the north wind, imagined as living in Thrace, the cold, horse-breeding land northeast of Greece.
Aphrodite is the goddess of love; the maiden is sheltered and has not yet experienced marriage.
Felt caps and cloaks of kidskin were ordinary rural winter wear; ox-sinew served as strong thread.

literary_notes.text: The crane 'vexes the heart' and gives signals like a person, making the bird a messenger of the seasons.
The daydreaming man 'rich in fancy' is sketched as a fool, a type of the idle farmer Hesiod warns against.
The balanced saying about good and bad management condenses the work ethic that runs through the poem.
Ears of corn bowing to the ground with fullness gives a vivid picture of an abundant harvest.
Hesiod admits that Zeus's will is hard to read, tempering his rules with humility about unpredictable divine control of nature.
Boreas acts like a violent being who falls on trees and makes the forest roar and beasts cower.
The old man bent "as a wheel" gives a vivid image of age and cold curving the body.
The warm, oiled maiden indoors is set against the freezing outdoors and the starving octopus, heightening the cold's severity.
Animals are compared to a bent old man with a staff, repeating the human image of fragility; "I say" adds a personal emphasis.
